chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Ya'qub ibn Yazid and Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Abdillah al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Abu Basir, who said:

I asked him about a man who married a woman and erred in not specifying a dowry for her, and then he consummated the marriage with her. He said: 'The Sunnah is the Sunnah, [which is] five hundred dirhams.'

And [I asked] about a man who married a woman during her waiting period [of a previous marriage], gave her the dowry, and then they were separated before he consummated the marriage with her. He said: 'He reverts to her with what he gave her.'

And he said: 'Which woman? A man marries her, and her husband has been announced to her [as deceased], but the second man has not yet consummated the marriage with her.' He said: 'She has no dowry, and it is an invalid marriage, and there is no waiting period for her to return to her first husband.'

key_terms.خَمْسُمِائَةِ دِرْهَمٍ: Five hundred dirhams, the standard amount for dowry in this context
key_terms.صَدَاقًا: Dowry or bridal gift given by the husband to the wife
key_terms.عِدَّةٌ: Waiting period a woman must observe after divorce or death of husband before remarrying
key_terms.مَهْرٌ: Dowry, specifically referring to the financial right of the wife
key_terms.نِكَاحٌ بَاطِلٌ: Invalid marriage, null and void from the beginning

ai.seo_question: What is the default dowry if not specified before consummation, and what happens to the dowry if the couple separates before consummation?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the default dowry (*sunnah*) of five hundred dirhams when unspecified, a ruling rooted in early Shia juristic consensus on equitable compensation. It further distinguishes between partial and full dowry retention upon separation before consummation and establishes that a marriage to a woman whose first husband is merely 'announced' (not yet divorced or consummated) is void (*batil*), exempting her from the waiting period (*iddah*). These rulings highlight the Shia emphasis on contractual clarity and the legal consequences of marital status ambiguity.
